references.text: Refers to how the woman (Eve) took the fruit and gave it to Adam, who then ate it – the event Adam refers to in his defense.
God brought the woman to Adam. In 3:12, Adam directly refers back to this: 'The woman whom you gave to be with me' – he indirectly blames God for giving him the woman.
Eve, on her part, blames the serpent, showing the same pattern of shifting responsibility that Adam displays in verse 12.
'Your first father sinned' – a reference to Adam as the first sinner, linking to the fall of Adam described in Gen 3:12.
Aaron blames the people for the golden calf and shifts responsibility, a pattern reminiscent of Adam's blame-shifting in the Garden of Eden.
'A man's folly leads him astray, but his heart is angry at the Lord' – describes the tendency to blame God for one's own mistakes, as Adam does in Gen 3:12.
The woman who in creation was man's joy and equal becomes in sin his excuse for ignoring his own responsibility.
